'''''Disphyma australe''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Aizoaceae]] and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to New Zealand. It is a [[Prostrate shrub|prostrate]], [[succulent plant|succulent]] [[Annual plant|annual]] shrub or short-lived [[perennial plant]] with stems up to {{cvt|2|m}} long, leaves that are three-sided in cross-section with a rounded lower angle, and white to deep pink daisy-like flowers<ref name="nzflora1" /><ref name="nzflora2" /> that are {{cvt|2 - 4|cm}} in diameter with 3–5 rows of [[petal]]s and multiple [[stamen]]s.<ref name="Webb1988" /> ''Disphyma australe'' is a coastal plant and therefore can be found at cliff faces, gravel beaches, salt meadows and estuaries.<ref name = "nzpcna" />

==Description==
''Disphyma australe'', the New Zealand ice plant, is a [[Succulent plant|succulent]] herb with a trailing or [[Prostrate shrub|prostrate]] habit,<ref name="Metcalf" /><ref name="Allan" /> which means that its branches usually spread along the ground. The stems are stout, about five millimeters in diameter and can be more than one meter long.<ref name="Allan" /> Especially old branches tend to be semi-woody.<ref name ="Metcalf" />
''Disphyma australe'' has triangular, fleshy leaves that are normally 2 – 4 cm long and circa 0.4 - 0.6 cm wide.<ref name="Webb1988">{{Cite book |title=Flora of New Zealand |last=Webb |first=C. J. |publisher=Botany Division |year=1988 |location=Christchurch |last2=Sykes |first2=W. R. |last3=Garnock-Jones |first3=P. J.}}</ref><ref name ="Metcalf" /> The shape of the leaves ́ tips ranges from pointed (acute) to rounded (obtuse), and their base is connotated. The leaves are arranged opposite one another.<ref name ="Metcalf" /><ref name="Allan" /> An important difference between ''Disphyma australe'' and the congener ''[[Disphyma papillatum|Dispyhma papillatum]]'' is the smooth leave surface of ''Disphyma australe'' in contrast to the roughed one of ''[[Disphyma papillatum]]''.<ref name ="Metcalf" />
[[File:Disphyma australe kz8.jpg|thumb|Flower]]
Another good feature for identifying the plant is its outstanding white or pink flowers, which have a diameter between 2 – 4 cm.<ref name="Webb1988" /><ref name ="Metcalf" /> Each flower sits at the end of a 1 – 4 cm [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]<ref name="Allan" /> and has many 1 – 3 cm [[petal]]s ordered in 3 - 5 rows.<ref name="Webb1988" /> Five lobes, two of them noticeably larger, form the succulent calyx. The reproductive organs of the plant consist of the female, 5 - 8 celled [[carpels]] including 5 - 8 styles<ref name="Allan" /> and usually 6 - 8 stigmas, and numerous male 4 – 6 mm long [[stamen]]s, which have filaments that are hairy at the bottom.<ref name="Webb1988" />

The fruits of ''Disphyma australe'' are fleshy, vase-shaped [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]] with some parallel silts, which allow the fruit to open, a flat end<ref name ="Metcalf" /> and wings. Each [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]] encloses the brown, rugose, oblong or egg-shaped,<ref name="Webb1988" /> 0.9 - 1.2 mm long seeds. They are compressed, with a slanted or cuneate, notched bottom and a rounded tip.<ref name =Webb2001 />

There are two subspecies of ''Disphyma australe'', ''Disphyma australe'' subsp. ''australe'' and subsp. ''stricticaule'', which differ only slightly in a few characteristics. Whereas ''D. australe'' has papillose [[sepal]] keels and placental [[tubercle]]s can be present, ''D. stricticaule'' has smooth [[sepal]] keels and no placental [[tubercle]]s.<ref name="Webb1988" />

== Range ==
[[File:Disphyma australe kz7.jpg|thumb|''Disphyma australe'' in [[Hāwera]] ([[Taranaki]], New Zealand)]]
''Disphyma australe'' is [[Endemism|endemic]] to New Zealand, that is, it occurs naturally only in New Zealand.<ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Webb1988" /> It now also grows on a few Australian islands, such as [[Tasmania]], [[Norfolk Island]] and [[Lord Howe Island]].<ref name = "Cheeseman">{{Cite book |title=Manual of the New Zealand Flora. |last=Cheeseman |first=T. F. |publisher=Skinner, W.A.G. |year=1925 |location=Wellington}}</ref>

The two subspecies of ''Disphyma australe'', ''D. australe australe'' and ''D. australe stricticaule'', are common in different parts of New Zealand.<ref name="Parsons" />
''D. australe stricticaule'' is only found on [[Kermadec Islands]],<ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Webb1988" /> whereas ''D. australe australe'' is found on both the North and South Island throughout the coast. It also occurs on some smaller New Zealand islands, like [[Stewart Island]], [[Chatham Islands]]<ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Allan" /> and [[Solander Islands]].<ref name="Parsons" /> Additionally, it coexists with ''D. australe stricticaule'' on the [[Kermadec Islands]].<ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Allan" />

==Habitat==
[[File:Disphyma australe kz11.jpg|thumb|Flowers and fruits]]
While ''Disphyma australe'' is rarely found inland,<ref name="nzpcna"/> it is very common at the coast.<ref name="Allan" /><ref name="nzpcna"/> It prefers especially rocky shores,<ref name = "Cheeseman" /> and both subspecies grow on cliff faces, rocks and on gravel and cobble beaches.<ref name = "nzpcna" /><ref name="Allan" /> Furthermore, it can also occur in other types of coastal habitats, including [[salt meadow]]s or [[Estuary|estuaries]]<ref name = "nzpcna" /><ref name= "Crowe" /> and occasionally at the back of sandy beaches.<ref name= "Crowe" /> Another place where ''Disphyma australe'' grows is near nesting grounds of sea birds, such as near [[petrel]] burrows,<ref name = "nzpcna" /><ref name= "Crowe" /> because in contrast to many other plants it can survive high amounts of bird droppings.<ref name= "Crowe" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Disphyma australe kz15.jpg|thumb|''Disphyma australe'' in [[Punakaiki]], [[Pancake Rocks and Blowholes|Pancake rocks]] ([[Westland, New Zealand|Westland]], New Zealand)]]

===Life cycle and phenology===
''Disphyma australe'' is a [[perennial plant]]  that can propagate either by seeds or by separated plant parts that can root again elsewhere.<ref name= "Crowe" /> Its flowers can be seen throughout the year,<ref name="Webb1988" /><ref name = "nzpcna" /> but mainly it blooms from spring to summer.<ref name="Webb1988" /><ref name="Metcalf" /> The flowers can turn with the sun<ref name= "Crowe" /> and, as the original name ''[[mesembryanthemum]]'' indicated, are mainly open at midday.<ref name = "Laing">{{Cite book |title=Plants of New Zealand. |last=Laing |first=R. M. |publisher=Whitcombe and Tombs Limited |year=1906 |location=Christchurch |last2=Blackwell |first2=E. W.}}</ref> Moreover, fruiting is typically between December and January,<ref name="Webb1988" /> although fruits can also be found from September to April.<ref name="Allan" /> As characteristic of the [[Aizoaceae]] family, the seeds are enclosed in [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]], which are closed during dry weather and open under wet or moist conditions,<ref name= "Crowe" /><ref name = "Laing" /> especially after heavy rainfall.<ref name="Webb1988" /> This phenomenon is called [[Dehiscence (botany)|hygrochasy]]<ref name="Webb2001" /> and occurs because the seeds germinate best on wet ground.<ref name= "Crowe" /> The mechanism still works when the plant is already dead.<ref name="Webb1988" /> Through wind, water or animals that eat the fruits of ''Disphyma australe'', the seeds can be dispersed in more distant places.<ref name = "nzpcna" />

===Diet and foraging===
As a coastal plant, which mainly grows on rocks and has the ability to store water, ''Disphyma australe'' favours dry, well-drained ground with direct sunshine,<ref name = "nzpcna" /><ref name= "Crowe" /> but has no particular preferences regarding [[soil fertility]]. Therefore, it is often found on gravel but can also be found on [[sandstone]] or [[limestone]] cliffs.<ref name = "nzpcna" /> Although most plants cannot tolerate high salt concentrations in the soil, studies show that ''Disphyma australe'' grows better when watered with water of moderate [[salinity]] instead of normal rainwater.<ref name = "Madawala">{{Cite magazine |title=Comparative growth and photosynthetic responses of native and adventive iceplant taxa to salinity stress |date=2014-10-02 |magazine=New Zealand Journal of Botany |last=Madawala |first=S. |doi=10.1080/0028825X.2014.925478|pages=352–364 |last2=Hartley |first2=S. |issue=3 |volume=52 |last3=Gould |first3=K. S.}}</ref> This corresponds with the statement that ''Disphyma australe'' is “prominent in the saltiest places”,<ref name= "Dawson" /> such as cliff faces and seashores, which are exposed to the salt spray of the ocean.<ref name = "Madawala" />

===Predators, parasites and diseases===
[[File:Melanostoma fasciatum 31177418.jpg|thumb|''[[Melanostoma fasciatum]]'', a pollinator of ''Disphyma australe'']]
Though there are few studies on the [[herbivore]]s of ''Disphyma australe'', some species that feed on the plant are known. Among them is the [[Hover fly|hoverfly]] ''[[Melanostoma fasciatum]]'', which pollinates ''Disphyma australe''. ''[https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/tools-and-resources/identification/what-is-this-bug/hibiscus-beetle/ Aethina concolor]'', however, is an [[Introduced species|adventive]], [[Herbivore|herbivorous]] beetle that eats the flowers.<ref name ="landcareb">{{Cite web |url=https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/ReportForm.aspx?RecordId=557&Type=P&ReportType=Adv&SortBy=Alpha&MinScore=|title=''Disphyma australe'' (W.T. Aiton) N.E. Br. (Host Plant). |access-date=1 March 2023|website=Landcare Research}}</ref> Another beetle that feeds on ''Disphyma australe'' is [[Holoparamecus|''Holoparamecus'' spp]].<ref name="Wise">{{Cite Q|Q58676879}}</ref> The leaves can be infested with sucking bugs such as the [[scale insect]]s ''[http://scalenet.info/catalogue/Poliaspis%20media/ Poliaspis media]'', which might cause galls on the underside of leaves, and the introduced ''[https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/discover-our-research/biodiversity-biosecurity/plants-invertebrates-fungi-and-bacteria/invertebrate-systematics/scale-insects/factsheets/pulvinaria-mesembryanthemi/ Pulvinaria mesembryanthemi]'', a bug specialised to host plants of the ''[[Mesembryanthemum]]'' family.<ref name ="landcareb" /> Additionally, larvae of the plantain moth (''[[Epyaxa rosearia|Xanthorhoe rosearia]]'') and the [[springtail]] species ''[[Hypogastrura]] rossi'' can be found on the plant.<ref name="Wise"/>

==Cultural uses==
<!--Note: Only include this if you found out information about this.-->
''Disphyma australe'' can be used in many ways. In addition to its use as a garden plant, it was primarily used as food and in medicine in the past. [[Māori people|Māori]] utilized the juice of the leaves for medical treatment, for example of boils,<ref name= "Crowe" /><ref name="Metcalf" /> abscesses, or itch. Recent studies show that ''Disphyma australe'' might have an anti-bacterial effect.<ref name ="Metcalf" /> European settlers ate the bland-tasting, fleshy capsules and pickled the leaves of ''Disphyma australe''.<ref name= "Crowe" />
